transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-09 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Clarke (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sara Nguyen (CTO, HavenPath), Diego Ramos (Platform Eng), Priya Menon (ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Customer wants p95 SLA guidance and a pilot for streaming clinical assistant; discuss Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs; follow-ups include benchmarks and cost sheet.

[00:00] Maya Clarke: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood and with me is Ethan our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Sara Nguyen: Good thanks, morning for me. Quick agenda — we want to make sure we cover p95 for streaming, concurrency burst, and also the security side.
[00:22] Ethan Park: Great, I can dive into runtime behavior and how we handle KV cache and streaming — disclaimer sometimes our transcript spells KV as K-V or K V.
[00:34] Diego Ramos: ha, yeah we saw a note about KV cache in the doc, curious how prefix caching works for repeated prompts.
[00:45] Maya: So top-level — are you leaning hosted, Dedicated, or Private? do you have regulatory constraints?
[00:52] Sara: We have HIPAA adjacency, not strictly patient PHI in the first phase but likely want SOC 2 and customer-managed KMS down the line. Private is on the table if costs and ops look reasonable.
[01:05] Priya Menon: For the product, it's a live clinical assistant. Typical session: user types, model streams tokens to UI, average reply length ~120 tokens, roughly 30 tokens/sec generation. We need p95 latencies around 350-450ms end-to-end for the first 60 tokens ideally.
[01:25] Ethan: Okay makes sense. Two things that impact p95: model selection and streaming path (token-by-token latency) and batching. For streaming with low latencies we avoid batching that adds batch wait time and use muxing/continuous batching with small windows.
[01:44] Sara: What's your baseline for a 4096-seq model or similar? we use a fine-tuned 7B variant for now.
[01:52] Ethan: For a 7B-ish architecture on a single A100-like GPU, token latency typically in the 20-80ms range depending on kv cache hit and kernel optimizations, but the end-to-end p95 for the first tokens often bumps due to cold start and HTTP stack. Our hosted environment has optimizations to keep WARM KVs and avoid cold starts.
[02:20] Liam O'Connor: Cold starts are our biggest scare. During burst events we could see many sessions spawn; how does Redwood handle concurrency and scaling?
[02:31] Maya: We have Dedicated pools where capacity is reserved — autoscaling policies let you keep a buffer for bursts. For Hosted we do per-tenant routing; fallbacks to smaller models if primary capacity exhausted. For Private you bring your own infra but you get same runtime and control plane.
[02:55] Diego: So in a burst, do you pre-provision instances or is it reactive? curious about p95 spikes.
[03:03] Ethan: You can configure a reserve (we call warm headrooms) — basically keep N ready copies of the model kernel and KV so cold-starts are rare. If you go pure reactive, p95 will spike during scale-outs.
[03:18] Sara: Let's talk numbers — our target is p95 < 450ms for streaming first 60 tokens across 4 concurrent sessions generating 30 tokens/sec each during a 10-minute burst window. Can Redwood meet that hosted?
[03:35] Ethan: Hosted probably yes, depending on model and region. We'll want to run a benchmark with your exact model and prompt set. For Dedicated with reserved capacity you'll have more deterministic p95; Private depends on your infra (network/VPC latency, NICs).
[03:55] Priya: For the benchmark we can provide tokenized prompt traces and some synthetic user timing patterns.
[04:02] Maya: Perfect — if you provide traces we'll run a token/sec baseline and p95 profiling. We'll also include a streaming trace so you can see tail latency contributions.
[04:15] Sara: When you say streaming traces — is that per-token latency breakdown? we want to know how much is service processing vs network/edge.
[04:24] Ethan: We'll instrument at request ingress, model step times, and egress. We'll show per-token latency and cumulative time. Note the network egress from private VPC can add variability.
[04:37] Diego: What about batching? If you use batching to reduce cost, will it impact our streaming p95?
[04:44] Ethan: Yes — batching improves tokens/sec and reduces unit cost but adds wait time. We usually use a hybrid: continuous batching with max latency SLA thresholds, and for streaming we keep batching windows very small (like 5-12ms) to preserve p95.
[04:58] Priya: Any quantization or kernel recs? we're on a custom fine-tuned 7B — curious about int8 and how it affects throughput/latency.
[05:08] Ethan: Quantization is a trade-off — int8 can increase throughput and lower cost, sometimes slightly increasing latency for per-token compute but often overall improves p95 because less memory pressure and better cache density. We'll recommend profiles after we see model artifacts.
[05:28] Sara: Security note — we need customer-managed KMS and audit logs. Can Hosted do KMS?
[05:36] Maya: Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer KMS for Enterprise tiers; Dedicated provides isolation and optional KMS integration, Private gives full control including on-prem HSM. We'll share the security pack.
[05:50] Liam: Also SSO and RBAC — we need SAML and fine-grained role controls.
[05:56] Maya: Yep, supported — we'll attach the docs.
[06:05] Ethan: Back to p95 — one more variable is concurrency per GPU. If you put too many sessions per instance, KV cache thrash and memory pressure can spike latencies. We usually recommend sizing so that sustained concurrency leaves 20-30% headroom.
[06:25] Diego: How do you recommend we size for our cited burst? 4 concurrent sessions is small but per-customer profile could be thousands of concurrent users.
[06:34] Ethan: For large fanout you want routing+sharding: per-region pools, and per-tenant isolation if needed. Also multi-tier fallback: if the heavy model can't meet p95 under load, route new sessions to a cheaper/fast variant while preserving quality.
[06:53] Sara: Is there an auto-fallback for streaming to a compressed model? we don't want to degrade clinical accuracy.
[07:00] Ethan: Fallback is configurable and policy-driven — you can failover to a quantized variant or a smaller model, or use per-request quality checks. For clinical use I'd be conservative: canary and A/B test first.
[07:15] Priya: About streaming — is there a recommended client-side strategy to render partial tokens and hide jitter?
[07:23] Ethan: Yes progressive rendering and smoothing buffers help. We'll share best-practice snippets and an SDK example for token buffering to reduce perceived latency.
[07:33] Sara: Can you walk through a sample benchmark plan? what will Redwood run and what we should expect as deliverables?
[07:40] Maya: We'll run three phases: 1) synthetic token/sec baseline with your prompts, 2) burst scenario with your fanout pattern and warm headroom configs, 3) cold-start and scale-up scenario. Deliverables: p50/p90/p95 token latency CSVs, token/sec throughput graphs, cost projection worksheet, and a short playback video showing timeline.
[08:05] Liam: What's realistic turnaround? we need results before our Jan roadmap review.
[08:10] Maya: If you upload traces by 2027-12-12 we'll run the benchmark and deliver results by 2027-12-15.
[08:18] Sara: Ok we'll try to meet that. A question on networking: if we run Private in our AWS region, will Redwood's control plane talk out-of-band? we need air-gapped options?
[08:29] Maya: Private can be air-gapped with an on-prem bundle; the control plane can be customer-hosted for air-gap scenarios but that adds deployment ops. We'll scope that if you move to Private.
[08:45] Diego: What's the cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated typically for our scale? idle buffer costs are my worry.
[08:53] Maya: We'll put numbers in the cost worksheet — Dedicated has predictable monthly commit for GPU capacity which reduces unit cost at scale; Hosted is pay-as-you-go but higher per-token. There's also a hybrid where you reserve baseline and burst to Hosted.
[09:10] Priya: For benchmarks, can we include real user think-times? latencies vary a lot when users type rapidly.
[09:17] Ethan: Absolutely, include real think-times and any pre-prompting that might warm KV (e.g., session history). That affects cache hit rates strongly.
[09:28] Sara: Any limits on token/sec per connection? and what about per-minute quotas that might throttle?
[09:35] Maya: There are per-connection bandwidth constraints but we expose token-rate throttles you can configure. For enterprise pilots we'll align quotas to avoid accidental throttles.
[09:48] Diego: Let's talk about instrumentation — we want traceable request IDs that map back to our logs.
[09:53] Ethan: We'll attach tracing hooks and an example of request-id propagation. Redwood Console will show per-token latency breakdowns and model-level metrics.
[10:06] Priya: If the model is fine-tuned, can caching still help? or does variance in outputs ruin prefix cache?
[10:12] Ethan: Caching helps when identical prefixes occur. For fine-tuned conversational models you often get repeated system prompts or instructions that cache well. We'll analyze your trace to estimate cache hit potential.
[10:27] Sara: Any notable risks we should be aware of for streaming p95?
[10:32] Ethan: Network variability, cold starts, and under-provisioned KV memory. Also large prompt lengths increase compute per token. We'll call these out in the benchmark report.
[10:44] Maya: Quick pause — I'm going to capture next steps. (brief silence)
[10:52] Maya: Action items as noted — we'll share cost worksheet, run benchmark, and you provide traces. Any other questions?
[11:00] Liam: One last: regulatory — retention windows for logs, can you redact PII automatically?
[11:06] Maya: We have opt-in retention policies and can integrate post-processing redaction; it's part of the Private/Enterprise pack.
[11:16] Priya: That should cover it. we're keen to see numbers.
[11:19] Sara: Thank you both. We'll aim to upload traces by Monday.
[11:24] Ethan: Great, we'll queue the benchmark and ping once results are ready.
[11:30] Maya: Thanks everyone — recap and I'll follow up with calendar invites for the results review.

(Transcript contains sporadic auto-caption errors; names and product features occasionally misspelled.)
